overview: This file consists of twelve Department of State “List of Papers” index sheets summarizing correspondence, telegrams, memoranda, intelligence reports, and cross-references concerning Japanese merchant-vessel movements in 1941 and 1942. The entries trace ships among Japanese, Asian, Pacific, North American, and South American ports; record cargoes, passengers, oil purchases, evacuations, searches, and requests for fuel; and document growing American, British, and Latin American concern that commercial vessels might support espionage, submarine operations, armed raiding, or preparations for war. Several entries also concern diplomatic passengers and Japanese claims that requisitioned liners should receive immunity from United States jurisdiction.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 48: entries 632–650
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries summarize reports on Japanese merchant vessels moving through Pacific and Latin American ports in July 1941.
subfiles.summary: The sheet indexes telegrams concerning the NO. WAY MARU, YAMAKAZE MARU, AKAGI MARU, KIYOKAWA, RAKUYO, NAKO, SHIRIYA, NISSYO, SYOYO, TAKAOKA MARU, KANSAI MARU, GAWA, BRISBANE MARU, MONETVIKKO MARU, NOZIMA MARU, NARUTO MARU, GINYO MARU, KUNIKAMA MARU, and SABAMI MARU. It also records Philippine oil-company sales to Japanese and French vessels and cross-references a report that the OKAGI MARU carried mercury, lead, molybdenum, mica, and flour from Manzanillo.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 49: entries 651–663
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes instructions and late-July reports concerning large Japanese ships and vessels operating between Japan, Latin America, Tahiti, and Australia.
subfiles.summary: One entry cross-references instructions requiring Yokohama, Kobe, and Osaka consular offices to telegraph movements of Japanese ships exceeding 4,000 gross tons. Other entries follow the GINYO MARU, HEIYO MARU, KIYOKAWA MARU, KUJOKAO MARU, YAKOGAWA, MARUTO MARU, CANBERRA, KASIMA, BUENOS AIRES MARU, TJISAROEA, and KUNA GAWA. Ecuadoran authorities searched one vessel for armament but reportedly found none.

subfiles.title: List of papers, sheet 50: entries 670–689
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: This index sheet combines August vessel reports with correspondence on Japanese shipping policy and financial alarm in London.
subfiles.summary: The entries track the SAKITO MARU, FUJIKAWA MARU, RAKUYO MARU, HEIYO MARU, HAVANA MARU, and other vessels at Latin American and Indian Ocean ports. A passenger list for the HEIYO MARU names Sobel, Hara, and Hitomi Teda. Additional correspondence concerns Japanese shipping policies, heavy sales of Japanese securities in London, and reports that Japanese ships had been ordered home.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 51: entries 671–684
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes vessel movements, oil sales, suspect cargoes, export disruption, and interdepartmental conversations about Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: Reports cover the YAMAZUKI or YAMAZAKI MARU, MANILA MARU, KIYAKAWA MARU, HEIYO MARU, ASUKA MARU, SAKITO MARU, MEXICO MARU, KOKKAI MARU, GANGES MARU, TATUTA MARU, HEIAN MARU, and DAISANGURU MARU. It records oil sales in the Philippines, cargo information from Buenos Aires, Rio de Janeiro, and Porto Alegre, and a suspension of Japanese exports to Panama attributed to a shortage of ships. Memoranda describe Takagi’s request for release of the YAMAZAKI MARU and a discussion with Hiss about Treasury information.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 52: entries 685½–699
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: The entries concern requests for fuel, vessel calls on the American Pacific coast, passengers, and a proposal for coastal patrols against Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: The sheet follows the AKAGI MARU, ASUKA MARU, KUNIKAWA MARU, HEIYO MARU, NOTO MARU, RAKUTO, BARATIA, and HISSY. A Manzanillo report identifies cargo, mail, two disembarking passengers, and the NOTO MARU’s proposed voyage to Callao, while a presidential referral encloses John Miscovich’s proposal for coastal patrols. Another entry notes unreliable or prematurely announced Japanese sailing dates.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 53: entries 700–715
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: This continuation indexes September and early-October reports on Japanese vessels traveling between Asian and American ports.
subfiles.summary: The entries concern the HEIYO MARU, TOYOOKA MARU, NORFOLK MARU, HOTO MARU, TOA MARU, NOTO MARU, AZUMA MARU, and other ships. They record arrivals, departures, destinations, cargo or supplies, and a vessel sailing to the United States with Nakasugi. Several lines are damaged or incomplete in the OCR, including an entry from the U.S. High Commissioner in the Philippines.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 54: entries 716–734
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: A badly degraded index sheet records passengers from the AZUMA MARU and additional vessel reports from Mexico, Wellington, Thailand, Yokohama, and Saigon.
subfiles.summary: The legible entry for the AZUMA MARU reports Japanese passengers and five Mexican diplomats returning from Japan and cross-references diplomatic files. Later entries identify reporting offices or officials at Mexico, Wellington, Antofagasta, Thailand, Yokohama, and Saigon, but most of their descriptive text is absent from the OCR. The sheet also cites a State Department memorandum by Bower and a U.S. naval attaché report from Mexico City.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 55: entries 736–751
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes October vessel movements, a Japanese requisitioned passenger ship, immunity requests, and naval intelligence reports.
subfiles.summary: Reports follow the NAN, FUTUNA, TATYO, NARUTO MARU, RUKKI, RAKUTO, and other vessels. One entry says a ship was requisitioned by Japan’s Ministry of Communications for Honolulu with 343 passengers and no cargo. The Japanese Embassy transmitted schedules and requested immunity from U.S. court jurisdiction, while Navy Department entries paraphrase reports from the 12th and 15th Naval Districts and the naval attaché at Rio.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 56: entries 753–772
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: This sheet follows Japanese ships and diplomatic passengers through Asian and Pacific ports during late October and November 1941.
subfiles.summary: Entries track the HEI MARU, TERUKAWA MARU, HIKAWA, TUKUBA MARU, LIMA MARU, HIE MARU, NARUTO MARU, ASAMA, NISSYO, TAKAHITO, and other vessels. They include information about Japanese diplomats reaching Acapulco, Philippine oil sales during September, and the TAKAHITO carrying 1,500 evacuees. Several place and ship names are severely corrupted in the OCR.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 57: entries 774–788
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: The entries document late-November and early-December ship movements, evacuation voyages, route verification, and Japanese claims of immunity.
subfiles.summary: Reports seek confirmation that Rangoon was the SINAI MARU’s previous port and trace the ASAMA, TAKACKA MARU, HUZISIMA, HUKEI, TATUTA, HIKAWA, TERUKAWA MARU, HUZI, and other vessels. Several ships carried or were expected to embark Japanese evacuees, and one vessel was ordered back to Japan. The final cross-reference states that the Secretary of State accepted Japanese representations supporting immunity for the TATUTA MARU, KIKAWA MARU, and TAYO MARU.

subfiles.title: List of papers, page 58: entries 790–802 and memorandum
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: This sheet indexes intelligence and correspondence from the immediate prewar and wartime transition, including hurried departures, suspected military uses, and Japanese preparations for war.
subfiles.summary: Two Japanese-crewed Argentine trawlers reportedly left Buenos Aires hastily on December 8 after British naval forces were warned. Other entries concern the TATUTA MARU’s expected arrival at Los Angeles, reports from TAIYO MARU passengers, gold aboard the TOA MARU, orders hastening the TERUKAWA MARU, and the possible conversion of the TOA MARU into an armed raider. Navy, Treasury, Justice, and private reports also address German ships under Japanese names and allegations that a vessel carried gasoline for submarines and aircraft.

subfiles.title: List of papers, list 59: entries 803–807
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: The final sheet supplies retrospective inquiries and memoranda concerning Japanese vessel movements during 1941 and the later whereabouts of particular ships.
subfiles.summary: A 1942 inquiry asks which Japanese vessel last carried cargo from Japan to the United States in 1941; the reply identifies the SYOYO MARU, which arrived at San Francisco on August 16. A State Department memorandum reviews Japanese shipping among the American republics, and a June 1942 communication discusses the ATAGO MARU’s March 1941 departure from Los Angeles and its possible whereabouts. A Justice Department entry references confidential information about Japanese ship movements.

interest: The file is especially useful as a finding aid to the State Department’s global surveillance of Japanese commercial shipping in the months before Pearl Harbor. It shows how apparently routine consular reports on arrivals, cargoes, fuel, and passengers became intertwined with naval intelligence, economic controls, diplomatic immunity, evacuation, and fears that merchantmen could become raiders or support submarines. Its geographic breadth and numerous cross-references can help historians reconstruct individual voyages and interagency information flows, while the garbled spellings also illustrate the care required when using OCR-derived archival indexes.
